claim: Zebrafish Tsp4b is 69% similar to human TSP4
source: Through an in situ expression screen for markers of muscle attachments, we identified a zebrafish tsp4, tsp4b (69% similar to human TSP4; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), which is expressed at all muscle attachment sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: The manuscript states a specific percentage of sequence similarity between zebrafish Tsp4b and human TSP4, which is a data-based comparison.

claim: Tsp4b is expressed at all muscle attachment sites in zebrafish
source: Through an in situ expression screen for markers of muscle attachments, we identified a zebrafish tsp4, tsp4b (69% similar to human TSP4; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), which is expressed at all muscle attachment sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ expression screen data and referenced figures showing expression patterns.

claim: Tsp4b contains a conserved CX2C motif (CQAC) identical to human TSP4 in its coiled-coil oligomerization domain
source: Similar to other subclass B Tsps, Tsp4b is predicted to be secreted as a pentamer as it contains a conserved CX2C motif (CQAC—Cys-Gln-Ala-Cys) identical to human TSP4 in its hydrophobic coiled-coil oligomerization domain (CCD) (25/36 residues are identical with human and mouse Tsp4), which is required for inter-subunit disulfide linkage (Efimov et al., 1994) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data showing the conserved motif and citation to prior work on disulfide linkage.

claim: 25/36 residues in the coiled-coil domain are identical between zebrafish Tsp4b and human and mouse Tsp4
source: Similar to other subclass B Tsps, Tsp4b is predicted to be secreted as a pentamer as it contains a conserved CX2C motif (CQAC—Cys-Gln-Ala-Cys) identical to human TSP4 in its hydrophobic coiled-coil oligomerization domain (CCD) (25/36 residues are identical with human and mouse Tsp4), which is required for inter-subunit disulfide linkage (Efimov et al., 1994) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific sequence comparison data.

claim: tsp4b mRNA is expressed throughout differentiating myotomes of embryonic somites beginning at 16 hpf
source: In situ analyses revealed tsp4b mRNA throughout the differentiating myotomes of embryonic somites beginning at 16 hr post fertilization (hpf, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing temporal and spatial expression patterns.

claim: tsp4b expression disappears in myoblasts as they differentiate
source: Expression disappears in myoblasts as they differentiate and by 60 hpf becomes restricted to putative tendon cells near somite boundaries and along the horizontal myoseptum (arrowheads in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) as well as at all muscle attachment sites of the head by 72 hpf (arrowheads in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal expression analysis from in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: By 60 hpf, tsp4b expression becomes restricted to putative tendon cells near somite boundaries and along the horizontal myoseptum
source: Expression disappears in myoblasts as they differentiate and by 60 hpf becomes restricted to putative tendon cells near somite boundaries and along the horizontal myoseptum (arrowheads in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) as well as at all muscle attachment sites of the head by 72 hpf (arrowheads in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data at specific developmental timepoints.

claim: tsp4b expression is detected at all muscle attachment sites of the head by 72 hpf
source: Expression disappears in myoblasts as they differentiate and by 60 hpf becomes restricted to putative tendon cells near somite boundaries and along the horizontal myoseptum (arrowheads in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) as well as at all muscle attachment sites of the head by 72 hpf (arrowheads in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing spatial expression patterns.

claim: The expression of tsp4b resembles that of tenomodulin (tnmd), a known tenocyte-specific marker
source: The expression of tsp4b resembles that of tenomodulin (tnmd), a known tenocyte-specific marker (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and their relatives are co-expressed in tendons and ligaments in humans (Docheva et al., 2005; Jelinsky et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative expression data and citations to prior work on tnmd and co-expression patterns.

claim: Tsp4b and tnmd relatives are co-expressed in tendons and ligaments in humans
source: The expression of tsp4b resembles that of tenomodulin (tnmd), a known tenocyte-specific marker (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and their relatives are co-expressed in tendons and ligaments in humans (Docheva et al., 2005; Jelinsky et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on human tendon and ligament gene expression.

claim: Down regulation of tsp4b in myotome occurs abruptly as the wave of muscle differentiation passes medio-laterally through each somite
source: Combined fluorescent localization of tsp4b mRNA and myosin heavy chain (MHC) protein revealed that down regulation of tsp4b in myotome occurs abruptly as the wave of muscle differentiation passes medio-laterally through each somite (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–H; Devoto et al., 1996; Henry et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined fluorescent localization data and citations to prior work on muscle differentiation.

claim: By 60 hpf, tsp4b expression was only detected in putative tenocytes along the somite boundaries, where muscle attachments have been established
source: By 60 hpf, tsp4b expression was only detected in putative tenocytes along the somite boundaries, where muscle attachments have been established (Figure 1—figure supplement 3I–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescent localization data at a specific developmental timepoint.

claim: Tsp4b protein localizes around the notochord and medial somite boundaries at 20 hpf
source: A polyclonal antibody raised against the unique N-terminus of zebrafish Tsp4b revealed extracellular protein localization around the notochord and medial somite boundaries at 20 hpf (Figure 1A–C) where myofibers of the axial musculature first elongate and attach, and this localization progressed laterally as more lateral fibers formed functional attachments at the somite boundary.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data using a specific antibody.

claim: Tsp4b protein localization progresses laterally as more lateral fibers form functional attachments at the somite boundary
source: A polyclonal antibody raised against the unique N-terminus of zebrafish Tsp4b revealed extracellular protein localization around the notochord and medial somite boundaries at 20 hpf (Figure 1A–C) where myofibers of the axial musculature first elongate and attach, and this localization progressed laterally as more lateral fibers formed functional attachments at the somite boundary.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing temporal and spatial progression of protein localization.

claim: By 72 hpf, Tsp4b protein was detected at the ends of all larval axial, appendicular, pharyngeal and extraocular muscles
source: By 72 hpf, Tsp4b protein was detected at the ends of all larval axial, appendicular, pharyngeal and extraocular muscles (Figure 1D–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing protein localization at multiple muscle types.

claim: In the cranial region, Tsp4b localizes to muscle-cartilage attachments, inter-muscular attachments, and muscle-soft tissue attachments
source: In the cranial region, these include muscle-cartilage attachments, inter-muscular attachments (between segments of the sternohyoideus [SH] muscle) and muscle-soft tissue attachments.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing protein localization at different types of cranial muscle attachments.

claim: During initial stages of muscle development in the trunk, myoblasts secrete their own Tsp4b to initiate attachment and MTJ assembly
source: These results suggest that during initial stages of muscle development in the trunk, myoblasts secrete their own Tsp4b to initiate attachment and MTJ assembly, and at later stages of somite muscle maturation, Tsp4b levels are maintained by secretion from tenocytes in mature MTJs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal and spatial expression patterns observed in the data.

claim: At later stages of somite muscle maturation, Tsp4b levels are maintained by secretion from tenocytes in mature MTJs
source: These results suggest that during initial stages of muscle development in the trunk, myoblasts secrete their own Tsp4b to initiate attachment and MTJ assembly, and at later stages of somite muscle maturation, Tsp4b levels are maintained by secretion from tenocytes in mature MTJs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal and spatial expression patterns observed in the data.

claim: Embryos injected with 0.32 ng/embryo of tsp4b-MO completely lacked Tsp4b protein by 72 hpf
source: Zebrafish embryos injected with antisense morpholino oligonucleotides (MOs) (0.32 ng/embryo) targeting the translation start site of tsp4b completely lacked Tsp4b protein by 72 hpf, as determined by whole-mount immunostaining with anti-Tsp4b.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data showing absence of protein after morpholino injection.

claim: tsp4b-MO injected embryos were slightly curved downward
source: tsp4b-MO injected embryos (hereafter referred to as Tsp4b-deficient) were slightly curved downward, but showed no defects in muscle morphology or swimming ability (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological observations of morpholino-injected embryos.

claim: tsp4b-MO injected embryos showed no defects in muscle morphology or swimming ability
source: tsp4b-MO injected embryos (hereafter referred to as Tsp4b-deficient) were slightly curved downward, but showed no defects in muscle morphology or swimming ability (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological and behavioral observations of morpholino-injected embryos.

claim: Muscle contractions induced with mild electrical stimulation caused dramatic muscle detachment in tsp4b-deficient embryos
source: However, muscle contractions induced with mild electrical stimulation caused dramatic muscle detachment in tsp4b-deficient embryos (Figure 2D–F,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electrical stimulation assays.

claim: Stimulation with repeated 8 millisecond pulses at 30 volts caused occasional isolated myofiber detachment in 23% (N = 16/68) of wild-type embryos
source: While stimulation with repeated 8 millisecond pulses at 30 volts caused the occasional isolated myofiber to detach in 23% (N = 16/68) of wild-type embryos, similar stimulation led to large portions of somites with detached fibers in 76% (N = 60/79) of tsp4b-deficient animals (Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from electrical stimulation experiments.

claim: Stimulation with repeated 8 millisecond pulses at 30 volts led to large portions of somites with detached fibers in 76% (N = 60/79) of tsp4b-deficient animals
source: While stimulation with repeated 8 millisecond pulses at 30 volts caused the occasional isolated myofiber to detach in 23% (N = 16/68) of wild-type embryos, similar stimulation led to large portions of somites with detached fibers in 76% (N = 60/79) of tsp4b-deficient animals (Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from electrical stimulation experiments.

claim: The muscle detachment phenotype was dependent on the strength of stimulation
source: Furthermore, this phenotype was dependent both on the strength of stimulation as well as the dose of tsp4b-MO (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data from electrical stimulation experiments.

claim: The muscle detachment phenotype was dependent on the dose of tsp4b-MO
source: Furthermore, this phenotype was dependent both on the strength of stimulation as well as the dose of tsp4b-MO (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data from morpholino injection experiments.

claim: The weakening of muscle attachments was specific to reduction of Tsp4b since it was partially rescued by injection of full-length tsp4b mRNA
source: This weakening of muscle attachments was specific to reduction of Tsp4b since it was partially rescued by injection of full-length tsp4b mRNA (Figure 2K).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data showing specificity of the morpholino effect.

claim: A mosaic distribution of exogenous mRNA restored Tsp4b protein specifically at the attachment sites of rescued myofibers in a dose-dependent manner
source: Furthermore, a mosaic distribution of exogenous mRNA restored Tsp4b protein specifically at the attachment sites of rescued myofibers in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2G–I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data from rescue experiments showing dose-dependent protein restoration.

claim: Wild-type embryos at 72 hpf showed basement membranes flanking a tightly packed electron dense MTJ (∼278 nm)
source: While wild-type embryos at 72 hpf showed basement membranes (BM) flanking a tightly packed electron dense MTJ (∼278 nm, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,E), both stimulated wild-type embryos and Tsp4b-deficient embryos prior to stimulation showed perturbation of the ECM at MTJs with intermittent separations of BM (∼423 nm and ∼527 nm, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data showing MTJ ultrastructure.

claim: Stimulated wild-type embryos showed perturbation of the ECM at MTJs with intermittent separations of BM (∼423 nm)
source: While wild-type embryos at 72 hpf showed basement membranes (BM) flanking a tightly packed electron dense MTJ (∼278 nm, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,E), both stimulated wild-type embryos and Tsp4b-deficient embryos prior to stimulation showed perturbation of the ECM at MTJs with intermittent separations of BM (∼423 nm and ∼527 nm, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data showing MTJ ultrastructure after stimulation.

claim: Tsp4b-deficient embryos prior to stimulation showed perturbation of the ECM at MTJs with intermittent separations of BM (∼527 nm)
source: While wild-type embryos at 72 hpf showed basement membranes (BM) flanking a tightly packed electron dense MTJ (∼278 nm, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,E), both stimulated wild-type embryos and Tsp4b-deficient embryos prior to stimulation showed perturbation of the ECM at MTJs with intermittent separations of BM (∼423 nm and ∼527 nm, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data showing MTJ ultrastructure in morpholino-injected embryos.

claim: Electrically stimulated Tsp4b-deficient embryos showed catastrophic defects in both ECM and BM integrity as well as a dramatic increase in MTJ separation (∼2668 nm)
source: In contrast, electrically stimulated Tsp4b-deficient embryos showed catastrophic defects in both ECM and BM integrity as well as a dramatic increase in MTJ separation (∼2668 nm, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D,E), while muscle fibers remained intact.
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data showing severe MTJ defects after stimulation.

claim: Muscle fibers remained intact in electrically stimulated Tsp4b-deficient embryos despite MTJ defects
source: In contrast, electrically stimulated Tsp4b-deficient embryos showed catastrophic defects in both ECM and BM integrity as well as a dramatic increase in MTJ separation (∼2668 nm, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D,E), while muscle fibers remained intact.
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data showing that muscle fiber structure is preserved despite MTJ failure.

claim: Tsp4b is required for maintenance and strengthening of MTJs
source: These results demonstrate a requirement for Tsp4b in maintenance and strengthening of MTJs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing MTJ defects in Tsp4b-deficient embryos.

claim: Early myofibers attach at somite boundaries by 20–24 hpf
source: During development of the axial musculature in zebrafish, early myofibers attach at somite boundaries by 20–24 hpf (Devoto et al., 1996), at least a day before tendon progenitors are detectable at somite boundaries by tsp4b mRNA expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work and temporal expression data.

claim: Tendon progenitors are detectable at somite boundaries at least a day after early myofibers attach
source: During development of the axial musculature in zebrafish, early myofibers attach at somite boundaries by 20–24 hpf (Devoto et al., 1996), at least a day before tendon progenitors are detectable at somite boundaries by tsp4b mRNA expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal expression data showing delayed appearance of tendon markers.

claim: Both isolated donor-derived wild-type muscle cells and putative tenocytes along somite boundaries restored Tsp4b protein and attachment of both donor and adjacent host myofibers (70%, N = 73)
source: Consistent with a requirement for Tsp4b in muscle attachment, both isolated donor-derived, wild-type muscle cells (Figure 3A–D), as well as putative tenocytes along somite boundaries (Figure 3E–H), restored Tsp4b protein and attachment of both donor and adjacent host myofibers (70%, N = 73), and these remained attached even when stimulated (Figure 3I–L; 40%, N = 51).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell transplantation experiments showing rescue of protein localization and function.

claim: Transplanted wild-type cells remained attached even when stimulated (40%, N = 51)
source: Consistent with a requirement for Tsp4b in muscle attachment, both isolated donor-derived, wild-type muscle cells (Figure 3A–D), as well as putative tenocytes along somite boundaries (Figure 3E–H), restored Tsp4b protein and attachment of both donor and adjacent host myofibers (70%, N = 73), and these remained attached even when stimulated (Figure 3I–L; 40%, N = 51).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell transplantation experiments with electrical stimulation.

claim: Tsp4b has a non cell-autonomous role in maintenance of muscle attachments
source: This demonstrates a non cell-autonomous role of Tsp4b in maintenance of muscle attachments.
evidence: The claim is inferred from cell transplantation experiments showing rescue of adjacent host cells.

claim: Zebrafish Tsp4b lacks an RGD motif but contains a non-canonical Itg-binding (KGD—Lys-Gly-Asp) motif in its C-terminus
source: Zebrafish Tsp4b lacks an RGD but contains a non-canonical Itg-binding (KGD—Lys-Gly-Asp) motif in its C-terminus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Ruoslahti, 1996; Adams, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data and citations to prior work on integrin-binding motifs.

claim: Tsp4b-deficient animals showed severe reductions in levels of activated focal adhesion kinase (FAK) detected with an antibody that recognizes phosphorylation at Tyrosine 861
source: Tsp4b-deficient animals showed severe reductions in key indicators of Itg signaling within myofibers. First, in 20–22 hpf embryos injected with tsp4b-MO, levels of activated focal adhesion kinase (FAK, detected with an antibody that recognizes phosphorylation at Tyrosine 861—pFAKy861) were dramatically reduced (Figure 4A–D,G), which was rescued by injection of tsp4b mRNA (Figure 4E–G; Henry et al., 2001), and at later stages (36 hpf) were mislocalized or lost in local regions along somite boundaries (Figure 4H–K), which was also rescued by co-injection of tsp4b mRNA (Figure 4L,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing reduced phosphorylated FAK levels.

claim: Reduced pFAK levels in Tsp4b-deficient embryos were rescued by injection of tsp4b mRNA
source: Tsp4b-deficient animals showed severe reductions in key indicators of Itg signaling within myofibers. First, in 20–22 hpf embryos injected with tsp4b-MO, levels of activated focal adhesion kinase (FAK, detected with an antibody that recognizes phosphorylation at Tyrosine 861—pFAKy861) were dramatically reduced (Figure 4A–D,G), which was rescued by injection of tsp4b mRNA (Figure 4E–G; Henry et al., 2001), and at later stages (36 hpf) were mislocalized or lost in local regions along somite boundaries (Figure 4H–K), which was also rescued by co-injection of tsp4b mRNA (Figure 4L,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data showing restoration of pFAK levels.

claim: At 36 hpf, pFAK was mislocalized or lost in local regions along somite boundaries in Tsp4b-deficient embryos
source: Tsp4b-deficient animals showed severe reductions in key indicators of Itg signaling within myofibers. First, in 20–22 hpf embryos injected with tsp4b-MO, levels of activated focal adhesion kinase (FAK, detected with an antibody that recognizes phosphorylation at Tyrosine 861—pFAKy861) were dramatically reduced (Figure 4A–D,G), which was rescued by injection of tsp4b mRNA (Figure 4E–G; Henry et al., 2001), and at later stages (36 hpf) were mislocalized or lost in local regions along somite boundaries (Figure 4H–K), which was also rescued by co-injection of tsp4b mRNA (Figure 4L,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing altered pFAK localization at later developmental stages.

claim: pFAK mislocalization in Tsp4b-deficient embryos was rescued by co-injection of tsp4b mRNA
source: Tsp4b-deficient animals showed severe reductions in key indicators of Itg signaling within myofibers. First, in 20–22 hpf embryos injected with tsp4b-MO, levels of activated focal adhesion kinase (FAK, detected with an antibody that recognizes phosphorylation at Tyrosine 861—pFAKy861) were dramatically reduced (Figure 4A–D,G), which was rescued by injection of tsp4b mRNA (Figure 4E–G; Henry et al., 2001), and at later stages (36 hpf) were mislocalized or lost in local regions along somite boundaries (Figure 4H–K), which was also rescued by co-injection of tsp4b mRNA (Figure 4L,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data showing restoration of pFAK localization.

claim: In regions where pFAK was mislocalized along the somite boundaries, muscle attachments appeared disorganized
source: In regions where pFAK was mislocalized along the somite boundaries, muscle attachments appeared disorganized.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological observations correlated with pFAK localization data.

claim: Simultaneous partial reduction of Tsp4b (sub-threshold doses of tsp4b-MO) and Itg signaling in heterozygous integrin-linked kinase (ilk+/−) mutants led to dramatic and widespread muscle detachment upon stimulation
source: Second, simultaneous partial reduction of Tsp4b (sub-threshold doses of tsp4b-MO) and Itg signaling in heterozygous integrin-linked kinase (ilk+/−) mutants, neither of which causes any detachment on its own, led to dramatic and widespread muscle detachment upon stimulation (Postel et al., 2008; Figure 4N).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction experiments showing synergistic effects.

claim: In Tsp4b-deficient embryos, expression and localization of a GFP-tagged Paxillin (Pxn)—Tg[Pxn-GFP] - was significantly reduced
source: Third, in Tsp4b-deficient embryos, expression and localization of a GFP-tagged Paxillin (Pxn)—Tg[Pxn-GFP] - was significantly reduced, indicating a severe reduction in Itg signaling within the myofibers themselves (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data from transgenic reporter lines.

claim: A Tg[Itga5-RFP] transgenic line showed specific localization of RFP at MTJs
source: In addition, a Tg[Itga5-RFP] transgenic line showed specific localization of RFP at MTJs, while Itga6-GFP localized more broadly along the entire length of each muscle fiber, which is reduced in Tsp4b-deficient embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data from transgenic reporter lines.

claim: Itga6-GFP localized more broadly along the entire length of each muscle fiber
source: In addition, a Tg[Itga5-RFP] transgenic line showed specific localization of RFP at MTJs, while Itga6-GFP localized more broadly along the entire length of each muscle fiber, which is reduced in Tsp4b-deficient embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data from transgenic reporter lines.

claim: Itga6-GFP localization is reduced in Tsp4b-deficient embryos
source: In addition, a Tg[Itga5-RFP] transgenic line showed specific localization of RFP at MTJs, while Itga6-GFP localized more broadly along the entire length of each muscle fiber, which is reduced in Tsp4b-deficient embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data comparing wild-type and Tsp4b-deficient embryos.

claim: Tsp4b functions as a ligand for muscle-specific Itgs at MTJs required to stabilize muscle attachments
source: These results are consistent with a functional role for Tsp4b as a ligand for muscle-specific Itgs at MTJs required to stabilize muscle attachments and point to Itga5 as one likely receptor.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data on integrin signaling and localization.

claim: Itga5 is a likely receptor for Tsp4b
source: These results are consistent with a functional role for Tsp4b as a ligand for muscle-specific Itgs at MTJs required to stabilize muscle attachments and point to Itga5 as one likely receptor.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the specific localization of Itga5-RFP at MTJs where Tsp4b is present.

claim: Injection of tsp4b-MO caused a reduction in localization of Lam at somite boundaries at 24 hpf
source: We found that injection of tsp4b-MO caused a reduction in localization of Lam at somite boundaries at 24 hpf (Figure 5A–D,G,N), which was rescued by co-injection of tsp4b mRNA (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing reduced laminin localization.

claim: Reduced Lam localization in Tsp4b-deficient embryos was rescued by co-injection of tsp4b mRNA
source: We found that injection of tsp4b-MO caused a reduction in localization of Lam at somite boundaries at 24 hpf (Figure 5A–D,G,N), which was rescued by co-injection of tsp4b mRNA (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data showing restoration of laminin localization.

claim: Reduced Lam localization correlated with disorganized muscle attachments
source: This correlated with disorganized muscle attachments.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological observations correlated with laminin localization data.

claim: At 36 hpf, Tsp4b-deficient embryos showed discontinuities in Lam distribution at somite boundaries
source: At later stages (36 hpf), Tsp4b-deficient embryos showed discontinuities in Lam distribution at somite boundaries (Figure 5H–K,N), with many fibers forming aberrant attachments at sites of localized Lam, which could be rescued by co-injection of tsp4b mRNA (Figure 5L,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing altered laminin distribution at later developmental stages.

claim: Many fibers formed aberrant attachments at sites of localized Lam in Tsp4b-deficient embryos
source: At later stages (36 hpf), Tsp4b-deficient embryos showed discontinuities in Lam distribution at somite boundaries (Figure 5H–K,N), with many fibers forming aberrant attachments at sites of localized Lam, which could be rescued by co-injection of tsp4b mRNA (Figure 5L,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological observations correlated with laminin localization data.

claim: Aberrant muscle attachments in Tsp4b-deficient embryos could be rescued by co-injection of tsp4b mRNA
source: At later stages (36 hpf), Tsp4b-deficient embryos showed discontinuities in Lam distribution at somite boundaries (Figure 5H–K,N), with many fibers forming aberrant attachments at sites of localized Lam, which could be rescued by co-injection of tsp4b mRNA (Figure 5L,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data showing restoration of normal muscle attachment patterns.

claim: lam mRNA (lama2, lamb1, lamc1, lamc2) levels were not significantly affected by tsp4b depletion
source: lam mRNA (lama2, lamb1, lamc1, lamc2) levels were not significantly affected by tsp4b depletion suggesting that these effects are post-transcriptional (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and most likely due to Tsp4b-Lam interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing no change in laminin transcript levels.

claim: The effects of Tsp4b depletion on laminin localization are post-transcriptional
source: lam mRNA (lama2, lamb1, lamc1, lamc2) levels were not significantly affected by tsp4b depletion suggesting that these effects are post-transcriptional (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and most likely due to Tsp4b-Lam interactions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that transcript levels are unchanged while protein localization is affected.

claim: The effects of Tsp4b depletion on laminin localization are most likely due to Tsp4b-Lam interactions
source: lam mRNA (lama2, lamb1, lamc1, lamc2) levels were not significantly affected by tsp4b depletion suggesting that these effects are post-transcriptional (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and most likely due to Tsp4b-Lam interactions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the post-transcriptional effects and prior knowledge of Tsp4-laminin interactions.

claim: In vitro binding assays using purified rat TSP4 have shown interactions with Lam, Col, and Fn among other ECM components
source: In vitro binding assays using purified rat TSP4 have shown interactions with Lam, Col, and Fn among other ECM components (Narouz-Ott et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work on TSP4 binding assays.

claim: Tsp4b could interact with Lam in a heteromeric complex and initiate an Itg signaling cascade necessary for maintenance of MTJs
source: Thus, Tsp4b could interact with Lam in a similar heteromeric complex, and initiate an Itg signaling cascade necessary for maintenance of MTJs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data on Tsp4b effects on laminin localization and integrin signaling, along with prior knowledge of TSP4-laminin interactions.

claim: Injecting the mutant form (KGD>KGE) of tsp4b mRNA failed to rescue the muscle detachment phenotype in Tsp4b-deficient embryos
source: To test requirements for this motif in promoting Itg activation in muscles, we designed a KGE mutant tsp4b mRNA (Figure 6A). Injecting the mutant form (KGD>KGE) of tsp4b mRNA failed to rescue the muscle detachment phenotype in Tsp4b-deficient embryos (Figure 6B), confirming a requirement for Itg binding in the function of Tsp4b.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data showing failure of the mutant to restore function.

claim: The KGD motif is required for Itg binding in the function of Tsp4b
source: To test requirements for this motif in promoting Itg activation in muscles, we designed a KGE mutant tsp4b mRNA (Figure 6A). Injecting the mutant form (KGD>KGE) of tsp4b mRNA failed to rescue the muscle detachment phenotype in Tsp4b-deficient embryos (Figure 6B), confirming a requirement for Itg binding in the function of Tsp4b.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the failure of the KGE mutant to rescue the phenotype.

claim: Subclass B Tsps function as pentamers through the highly conserved 36 residue coiled-coil motif
source: Subclass B Tsps function as pentamers through the highly conserved 36 residue coiled-coil motif (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about thrombospondin structure and function.

claim: Both SQAS-gfp and tsp4b-gfp were expressed similarly and strongly fluorescent at 7–8 hpf
source: To verify SQAS-gfp mRNA expression, we injected wild type tsp4b-gfp and SQAS-gfp into one-cell stage embryos and analyzed them for expression at gastrula stages. Both SQAS-gfp and tsp4b-gfp were expressed similarly and strongly fluorescent at 7–8 hpf, suggesting that the mutated SQAS protein is synthesized and secreted (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data showing similar expression levels of wild-type and mutant constructs.

claim: The mutated SQAS protein is synthesized and secreted
source: To verify SQAS-gfp mRNA expression, we injected wild type tsp4b-gfp and SQAS-gfp into one-cell stage embryos and analyzed them for expression at gastrula stages. Both SQAS-gfp and tsp4b-gfp were expressed similarly and strongly fluorescent at 7–8 hpf, suggesting that the mutated SQAS protein is synthesized and secreted (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of fluorescence at early stages.

claim: At later stages, tsp4b-gfp localized to MTJs similar to wild-type Tsp4b
source: However, at later stages while tsp4b-gfp localized to MTJs similar to wild-type Tsp4b, SQAS-gfp fluorescence was not localized and gradually disappeared (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data showing localization of the GFP-tagged wild-type protein.

claim: SQAS-gfp fluorescence was not localized and gradually disappeared at later stages
source: However, at later stages while tsp4b-gfp localized to MTJs similar to wild-type Tsp4b, SQAS-gfp fluorescence was not localized and gradually disappeared (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data showing loss of the mutant protein over time.

claim: SQAS-gfp failed to localize to MTJs in Tsp4b-deficient embryos, in contrast to tsp4b-FLAG mRNA
source: SQAS-gfp also failed to localize to MTJs in Tsp4b-deficient embryos, in contrast to tsp4b-FLAG mRNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data comparing mutant and wild-type constructs in Tsp4b-deficient embryos.

claim: Tsp4b-FLAG and Tsp-GFP predominantly existed as pentamers
source: A western blot of the protein extract showed that Tsp4b-FLAG and Tsp-GFP predominantly existed as a pentamers, while SQAS-GFP was exclusively present as monomers, further confirming that the oligomerization function of Tsp4b mediated by CQAC motif of CCD is essential for localization of Tsp4b to the MTJ (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data under non-reducing conditions showing high molecular weight bands.

claim: SQAS-GFP was exclusively present as monomers
source: A western blot of the protein extract showed that Tsp4b-FLAG and Tsp-GFP predominantly existed as a pentamers, while SQAS-GFP was exclusively present as monomers, further confirming that the oligomerization function of Tsp4b mediated by CQAC motif of CCD is essential for localization of Tsp4b to the MTJ (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data under non-reducing conditions showing low molecular weight bands.

claim: The oligomerization function of Tsp4b mediated by CQAC motif of CCD is essential for localization of Tsp4b to the MTJ
source: A western blot of the protein extract showed that Tsp4b-FLAG and Tsp-GFP predominantly existed as a pentamers, while SQAS-GFP was exclusively present as monomers, further confirming that the oligomerization function of Tsp4b mediated by CQAC motif of CCD is essential for localization of Tsp4b to the MTJ (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing that the SQAS mutant fails to form pentamers and fails to localize to MTJs.

claim: Wild type embryos injected with the SQAS form of tsp4b mRNA showed significantly increased muscle detachment upon stimulation compared to controls
source: To test requirements for oligomerization of Tsp4b in muscle attachment, ECM organization and Itg signaling we injected wild type embryos with the SQAS form of tsp4b mRNA. Injected larvae at 3 dpf showed significantly increased muscle detachment upon stimulation compared to controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrical stimulation experiments showing increased detachment with the SQAS mutant.

claim: When co-injected with the tsp4b MO, the SQAS tsp4b mRNA failed to rescue muscle detachment
source: Furthermore, when co-injected with the tsp4b MO, the SQAS tsp4b mRNA failed to rescue muscle detachment (Figure 6B), FAK activation or Lam localization at MTJs (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data showing failure of the SQAS mutant to restore function.

claim: The SQAS tsp4b mRNA failed to rescue FAK activation at MTJs
source: Furthermore, when co-injected with the tsp4b MO, the SQAS tsp4b mRNA failed to rescue muscle detachment (Figure 6B), FAK activation or Lam localization at MTJs (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing lack of pFAK restoration with the SQAS mutant.

claim: The SQAS tsp4b mRNA failed to rescue Lam localization at MTJs
source: Furthermore, when co-injected with the tsp4b MO, the SQAS tsp4b mRNA failed to rescue muscle detachment (Figure 6B), FAK activation or Lam localization at MTJs (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing lack of laminin restoration with the SQAS mutant.

claim: Pentameric Tsp4b is a key scaffolding component that is required for MTJ ECM assembly and muscle-specific Itg signaling
source: These results suggest that in addition to a requirement for its own assembly and localization at MTJs, pentameric Tsp4b is a key scaffolding component that is required for MTJ ECM assembly and muscle-specific Itg signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing that pentamerization is required for Tsp4b function in ECM organization and integrin signaling.

claim: Studies of bovine, equine and human TSP4 have shown that it localizes to tendons
source: Studies of bovine, equine and human TSP4 have shown that it localizes to tendons (Hauser et al., 1995; Chen et al., 2000; Södersten et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work on TSP4 localization in various species.

claim: Exogenous TSP4 protein localized to MTJs adjacent to the site of injection
source: Exogenous TSP4 protein localized to MTJs adjacent to the site of injection and rescued muscle detachment in Tsp4b-deficient larvae when stimulated (22% detached [N = 136] compared to 52% detached [N = 96] in stimulated Tsp4b-deficient embryos) (Figure 7A–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing localization of injected human TSP4 protein.

claim: Exogenous TSP4 protein rescued muscle detachment in Tsp4b-deficient larvae when stimulated (22% detached [N = 136] compared to 52% detached [N = 96] in stimulated Tsp4b-deficient embryos)
source: Exogenous TSP4 protein localized to MTJs adjacent to the site of injection and rescued muscle detachment in Tsp4b-deficient larvae when stimulated (22% detached [N = 136] compared to 52% detached [N = 96] in stimulated Tsp4b-deficient embryos) (Figure 7A–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from electrical stimulation experiments with injected human TSP4.

claim: Injection of exogenous TSP4 protein reduced the occurrence of muscle detachments by ∼20% in wild-type embryos electrically stimulated with increasing voltages
source: In addition, injection of exogenous TSP4 protein reduced the occurrence of muscle detachments by ∼20% in wild-type embryos (N = 40 embryos) electrically stimulated with increasing voltages (Figure 7J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from electrical stimulation experiments showing protective effects of TSP4.

claim: TSP4 and zebrafish Tsp4b are both structurally and functionally similar
source: These results suggest that TSP4 and zebrafish Tsp4b are both structurally and functionally similar, and that TSP4 also serves as a scaffold for ECM assembly at MTJs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the ability of human TSP4 to rescue zebrafish Tsp4b deficiency.

claim: TSP4 serves as a scaffold for ECM assembly at MTJs
source: These results suggest that TSP4 and zebrafish Tsp4b are both structurally and functionally similar, and that TSP4 also serves as a scaffold for ECM assembly at MTJs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the functional rescue experiments with human TSP4.

claim: Vertebrate tendons consist of a complex network of collagen-rich fibrils, which interact with other ECM proteins and membrane adhesion complexes on the surfaces of muscle cells to form attachments strong enough to bear contractile forces
source: Vertebrate tendons consist of a complex network of collagen-rich fibrils, which interact with other ECM proteins and membrane adhesion complexes on the surfaces of muscle cells to form attachments strong enough to bear contractile forces (Ros et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work and represents established knowledge about tendon structure.

claim: Muscles of the embryonic zebrafish undergo dynamic changes in ECM composition
source: Muscles of the embryonic zebrafish undergo dynamic changes in ECM composition (Henry et al., 2001; Crawford et al., 2003; Snow and Henry, 2009; Sen et al., 2011), in which early high levels of Fn are replaced by Lams and Cols and later by an orthogonal array of collagen fibrils (Kannus, 2000; Câmara-Pereira et al., 2009; Charvet et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work on zebrafish muscle ECM development.

claim: Early high levels of Fn are replaced by Lams and Cols and later by an orthogonal array of collagen fibrils in zebrafish muscle ECM
source: Muscles of the embryonic zebrafish undergo dynamic changes in ECM composition (Henry et al., 2001; Crawford et al., 2003; Snow and Henry, 2009; Sen et al., 2011), in which early high levels of Fn are replaced by Lams and Cols and later by an orthogonal array of collagen fibrils (Kannus, 2000; Câmara-Pereira et al., 2009; Charvet et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work on temporal changes in ECM composition.

claim: Changes in ECM are critical for muscle attachment and maturation of MTJs
source: These changes in ECM are critical for muscle attachment and maturation of MTJs.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about the importance of ECM dynamics in muscle development.

claim: Zebrafish Tsp4b is essential for muscle attachment and ECM assembly at myotendinous junctions (MTJs)
source: We show for the first time that a vertebrate thrombospondin, Tsp4b, is essential for muscle attachment and ECM assembly at myotendinous junctions (MTJs).
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined experimental data showing defects in muscle attachment and ECM organization in Tsp4b-deficient embryos.

claim: Tsp4b depletion in zebrafish causes muscle detachment upon contraction due to defects in laminin localization and reduced Itg signaling at MTJs
source: Tsp4b depletion in zebrafish causes muscle detachment upon contraction due to defects in laminin localization and reduced Itg signaling at MTJs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined experimental data showing laminin mislocalization and reduced integrin signaling in Tsp4b-deficient embryos.

claim: Mutation of the oligomerization domain renders Tsp4b unable to rescue muscle detachment defects
source: Mutation of its oligomerization domain renders Tsp4b unable to rescue these defects, demonstrating that pentamerization is required for ECM assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that the SQAS mutant fails to restore function.

claim: Pentamerization is required for ECM assembly at MTJs
source: Mutation of its oligomerization domain renders Tsp4b unable to rescue these defects, demonstrating that pentamerization is required for ECM assembly.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the failure of the oligomerization-deficient mutant to rescue ECM defects.

claim: Injected human TSP4 localizes to zebrafish MTJs
source: Furthermore, injected human TSP4 localizes to zebrafish MTJs and rescues muscle detachment and ECM assembly in Tsp4b-deficient embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing localization of injected human TSP4.

claim: Injected human TSP4 rescues muscle detachment in Tsp4b-deficient embryos
source: Furthermore, injected human TSP4 localizes to zebrafish MTJs and rescues muscle detachment and ECM assembly in Tsp4b-deficient embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrical stimulation experiments showing reduced detachment after TSP4 injection.

claim: Injected human TSP4 rescues ECM assembly in Tsp4b-deficient embryos
source: Furthermore, injected human TSP4 localizes to zebrafish MTJs and rescues muscle detachment and ECM assembly in Tsp4b-deficient embryos.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the functional rescue of muscle attachment, which depends on proper ECM assembly.

claim: Tsp4 functions as an ECM scaffold at MTJs
source: Thus Tsp4 functions as an ECM scaffold at MTJs, with potential therapeutic uses in tendon strengthening and repair.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing Tsp4b's role in organizing ECM components and maintaining MTJ integrity.

claim: Tsp4 has potential therapeutic uses in tendon strengthening and repair
source: Thus Tsp4 functions as an ECM scaffold at MTJs, with potential therapeutic uses in tendon strengthening and repair.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the ability of exogenous TSP4 to strengthen MTJs and rescue defects.

claim: Pentameric Tsp4 in vivo functions as a scaffold to assemble other ECM components, and their interactions with Itgs and Dys complexes at MTJs
source: We propose a model in which pentameric Tsp4 in vivo functions as a scaffold to assemble other ECM components, and their interactions with Itgs and Dys complexes at MTJs (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the combined experimental data and prior knowledge of ECM interactions.

claim: Human TSP4 forms pentamers
source: Human TSP4, which forms pentamers (Lawler et al., 1995; Frolova et al., 2012), is also capable of rescuing Tsp4b-deficient zebrafish, demonstrating that the two are functionally interchangeable.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work on human TSP4 structure.

claim: Human TSP4 is functionally interchangeable with zebrafish Tsp4b
source: Human TSP4, which forms pentamers (Lawler et al., 1995; Frolova et al., 2012), is also capable of rescuing Tsp4b-deficient zebrafish, demonstrating that the two are functionally interchangeable.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that human TSP4 can substitute for zebrafish Tsp4b.

claim: The C-terminal region of mammalian Tsp5 has been suggested to interact with multiple ECM proteins in cartilage
source: The C-terminal region of mammalian Tsp5, which also functions as a pentamer, has been suggested to interact with multiple ECM proteins in cartilage (Hecht et al., 1998; Chen et al., 2007) and with collagen fibrils in tendons (Chen et al., 2007; Södersten et al., 2007; Tan and Lawler, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work on Tsp5 interactions.

claim: The C-terminal region of mammalian Tsp5 has been suggested to interact with collagen fibrils in tendons
source: The C-terminal region of mammalian Tsp5, which also functions as a pentamer, has been suggested to interact with multiple ECM proteins in cartilage (Hecht et al., 1998; Chen et al., 2007) and with collagen fibrils in tendons (Chen et al., 2007; Södersten et al., 2007; Tan and Lawler, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work on Tsp5 interactions.

claim: Tsp4 serves as a central organizing factor in MTJs by interacting with multiple ECM proteins, proteoglycans and receptors on muscle membranes
source: We hypothesize that Tsp4 serves as a central organizing factor in MTJs by interacting with multiple ECM proteins, proteoglycans and receptors on muscle membranes.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the experimental data and prior knowledge of Tsp4 interactions.

claim: Other Tsps could play similar organizational roles as pentamers (subclass B) or trimers (subclass A) in contexts where they are required such as neurite outgrowth, synapse formation, wound healing and tumorigenesis
source: Other Tsps could play similar organizational roles as pentamers (subclass B) or trimers (subclass A) in contexts where they are required such as neurite outgrowth, synapse formation, wound healing and tumorigenesis (Arber and Caroni, 1995; Kyriakides et al., 1998, 1999; Sid et al., 2004; Christopherson et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is speculative, extrapolating from the findings on Tsp4b to other thrombospondins, with support from citations to prior work.

claim: Axial muscles attach directly to the basement membrane at somite boundaries in the early embryo and become contractile and functional at least 12 hr before tenocytes are detected at MTJs
source: Axial muscles attach directly to the basement membrane at somite boundaries in the early embryo and become contractile and functional at least 12 hr before tenocytes are detected at MTJs (Devoto et al., 1996; Barresi et al., 2001; Henry et al., 2005; Snow and Henry, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work on zebrafish muscle development.

claim: After axial muscle progenitors attach, they secrete their own Tsp4b, which they downregulate upon differentiation, while later Tsp4b is secreted and maintained by tenocytes
source: Our results suggest that after axial muscle progenitors attach, they secrete their own Tsp4b, which they downregulate upon differentiation, while later Tsp4b is secreted and maintained by tenocytes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal and spatial expression patterns of tsp4b observed in the data.

claim: Tenocytes in the zebrafish trunk likely originate from the syndetome compartment in each somite, similar to their counterparts in the chick, and migrate to sites of muscle attachment
source: Tenocytes in the zebrafish trunk likely originate from the syndetome compartment in each somite, similar to their counterparts in the chick, and migrate to sites of muscle attachment (Brent et al., 2003; Shukunami et al., 2006; Chen and Galloway, 2014).
evidence: The claim is inferred from prior work on tendon development in other species, with support from citations.

claim: Tsp4b expression is observed in cranial tenocytes at MTJs but not in cranial muscles
source: In contrast, we observe Tsp4b expression in cranial tenocytes at MTJs but not in cranial muscles.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing differential expression patterns between cranial and axial muscles.

claim: There are distinct types of interactions between myoblasts and tenocytes involved in forming different types of MTJs
source: This difference in the timing and sources of Tsp4b between cranial and axial muscles suggests that there are distinct types of interactions between myoblasts and tenocytes involved in forming different types of MTJs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed differences in Tsp4b expression patterns between cranial and axial muscles.

claim: Tsp4b is required for both initial attachments of some early muscles and more broadly in the maintenance of all types of attachments
source: Our results suggest that Tsp4b is required for both initial attachments of some early muscles, which correlates with defects in early ECM, as well as more broadly in the maintenance of all types of attachments.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing defects at different developmental stages and in different muscle types.

claim: Tsp4−/− mice show progressive weight loss, atrophy of muscle mass and disrupted packing of collagen fibrils, but they are viable and fertile
source: Tsp4−/− mice show progressive weight loss, atrophy of muscle mass and disrupted packing of collagen fibrils, but they are viable and fertile (Frolova et al., 2010, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work on Tsp4 knockout mice.

claim: Tsp4b-deficient zebrafish appear largely unaffected until their muscles are subjected to multiple contractions
source: Similarly, Tsp4b-deficient zebrafish appear largely unaffected until their muscles are subjected to multiple contractions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations showing normal morphology and behavior until stimulation.

claim: TSP4 is upregulated in response to exercise, myocardial infarction and in several types of muscular dystrophy
source: For example, TSP4 (and other Tsps) is upregulated in response to exercise, myocardial infarction and in several types of muscular dystrophy (Chen et al., 2000; Timmons et al., 2005; Frolova et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work on TSP4 expression in response to stress.

claim: Tsp5 expression is elevated in response to biomechanical stress
source: Tsp5 expression is elevated in response to biomechanical stress (Hecht et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work on Tsp5 expression.

claim: Subclass A Tsps (Tsp 1–2) are elevated in response to injury or inflammation
source: Subclass A Tsps (Tsp 1–2) are also elevated in response to injury or inflammation (Bornstein et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work on subclass A thrombospondins.

claim: Elevated Tsp expression in response to stress could reflect an attempt by cells at ECM repair but may also be detrimental by causing tissue fibrosis
source: Elevated Tsp expression in all these scenarios could reflect an attempt by cells at ECM repair but may also be detrimental by causing tissue fibrosis.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential dual roles for elevated Tsp expression.

claim: In Tsp2−/− mutant mice, wound healing progresses rapidly without scarring, but with abnormal Col fibril structure
source: Consistent with this idea, in Tsp2−/− mutant mice, wound healing progresses rapidly without scarring, but with abnormal Col fibril structure (Kyriakides et al., 1998; Bornstein et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work on Tsp2 knockout mice.

claim: Tsp4−/− mice show elevated levels of Col (Col I, II, III, V) in the heart
source: Tsp4−/− mice show elevated levels of Col (Col I, II, III, V) in the heart.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about Tsp4 knockout mice from prior studies.

claim: Elevated accumulation of Col in Tsp4−/− mice is reversed with application of TSP4 in an in vitro cell culture system
source: This elevated accumulation of Col is reversed with application of TSP4 in an in vitro cell culture system (Frolova et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work on TSP4 function in cell culture.

claim: The scaffolding function of Tsp4 is evolutionarily conserved and functions as a modulator of ECM organization in multiple tissue types
source: This result is similar to our in vivo study, where injected TSP4 rescues the Tsp4b-deficient phenotype, suggesting that the scaffolding function of Tsp4 is evolutionarily conserved and functions as a modulator of ECM organization in multiple tissue types.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the functional rescue experiments and comparison with prior work on TSP4 in other tissues.

claim: Tsp4 localized to the endoplasmic reticulum of cardiac fibroblasts promotes nuclear shuttling of activating transcription factor 6 alpha
source: Recent work on the functions of Tsp4 in cardiac ECM has shown interesting intracellular functions, where Tsp4 localized to the endoplasmic reticulum of cardiac fibroblasts promotes nuclear shuttling of activating transcription factor 6 alpha (Lynch et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work on intracellular Tsp4 functions.

claim: The ability of exogenous TSP4 protein injected extracellularly to rescue a Tsp4b-deficient phenotype suggests that the primary function of Tsp4 is in ECM organization at MTJs
source: While this intracellular role of Tsp4 cannot be ruled out in MTJ organization, the ability of exogenous TSP4 protein injected extracellularly to rescue a Tsp4b-deficient phenotype suggests that the primary function of Tsp4 is in ECM organization at MTJs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that extracellular TSP4 is sufficient to restore function.

claim: A mouse model for congenital muscular dystrophy caused by Lama2 deficiency can be treated effectively by injecting recombinant Laminin1-1-1 trimer
source: A mouse model for congenital muscular dystrophy caused by Lama2 deficiency can be treated effectively by injecting recombinant Laminin1-1-1 trimer (Rooney et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work on laminin therapy in mice.

claim: The strategy of treating myotendinopathies by injecting recombinant ECM proteins is a viable option
source: Hence, the strategy of treating such 'myotendinopathies' by injecting recombinant ECM proteins is a viable option.
evidence: The claim is inferred from prior work on laminin therapy and the current findings with TSP4.

claim: TSP4 has potential use in promoting efficient tendon and MTJ repair and correcting defects in the ECM in a whole range of myotendinopathies
source: Our work provides a potential new therapeutic strategy using TSP4 to promote efficient tendon and MTJ repair and correcting defects in the ECM in a whole range of myotendinopathies.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential therapeutic applications based on the experimental findings.
